#3187. The Novilla Bliss is an Amazon best-seller, but is this memory foam mattress worth it? I slept on the budget bed for a month to find out

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Novilla Bliss Memory Foam is an all-foam mattress that’s particularly suited to side sleepers and lightweight back sleepers. I slept on a Full size 10" mattress for a month, along with my husband, and I found it especially comfortable for side sleeping. I was also really impressed with the support it provided, considering its low price. But support at the edges left a lot to be desired and it won't be supportive enough for heavier sleepers, and my hot-sleeping husband found it slept way too warm, too.

Far more supportive than its price would suggest

Not robust enough for stomach sleepers or those over 230lbs

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Insanely popular on Amazon, the Novilla Bliss Memory Foam Mattress is a cheap and cheerful all-foam offering that I freely admit I wasn’t expecting much from. However, there were lots of things about the Novilla Bliss that surprised me in a good way and overall, I was quite impressed by the support considering the mattress’ very reasonable pricing.

Name: Jo PlumridgeAge bracket: 45-55Weight bracket: 100-130lbsPredominant sleep position: Combination sleeper who spends slightly more time on her sideSleep issues: Suffers with back pain which can easily be exacerbated by an unsupportive mattress

It’s not going to rival the very best mattresses on the market but if you’re on a budget, this should definitely be on your radar. With a queen mattress currently priced at $269.99 in the Black Friday mattress deals, I think this is one of the best budget beds currently on the market.

In terms of firmness, I’d suggest that most sleepers will find it at the firmer end of the medium scale. There is sinkage and this is an all-foam mattress, but there’s still some support underneath. I can’t think of any other all-foam mattresses I’ve slept on that are as firm, except for the Nectar Classic Memory Foam. However, I must stress that I’m a lightweight sleeper and my husband, who is lightweight to average weight for a man, found it softer than I did.

Still, we both enjoyed it for side sleeping particularly and, as someone who is ultra fussy about lumbar support, I found it more comfortable for back sleeping than I expected. Motion isolation on the Novilla Bliss is exceptional, and I couldn’t feel my husband moving around at all, but edge support is lacking both when you lie or sit on the edge. I didn’t feel as if I’d actually fall off the bed, but there was some definite tilting.

Type: Memory FoamFirmness: Medium (lighter sleepers will find it medium firm)Height: 10"Trial period: 100 nightsWarranty: 10 yearsPrice: From $179.99 at Novilla

The mattress' one big failing, though, is temperature regulation. I sleep cold so this wasn't an issue, but my husband found it stuffy and, while he didn't wake up sweaty, he didn’t find it massively comfortable either. Hot sleepers on a budget might be happier on the Siena 10" Signature mattress, which kept our testers comfortably cool. But value for money is the Novilla Bliss' big selling point and considering its price, I was really impressed overall with the mattress.

Read on for my full assessment of the Novilla Bliss Memory Foam mattress so you can decide if it’s worth investing in.

A queen size Novilla Bliss is listed at $269.99 with a 20% discount from $337.99 on the brand’s own website, while Amazon currently has the price at $269.99. This sale price seems to be fairly set, so here are the MSRPs for each size, plus the usual sale price you can expect to pay:

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Of course, November is one of the best times of the year for mattress sales and we’re seeing some Black Friday deals — a twin size Novilla 8" hybrid mattress is down to $90, for example, and on Amazon the queen size 10" Novilla Bliss has dropped below $210 a couple of times in 2026. So, it’s definitely worth keeping an eye on prices but do remember that, at $269.99 for a queen, the Novilla Bliss is already incredibly well priced.

Benefits differ very slightly depending on where you buy the mattress. On the brand’s own site, you’ll bet a 100-night trial, 10-year warranty and free shipping and returns. Amazon, on the other hand, offers a 90-night easy returns system, manufacturer’s warranty and free shipping and returns.

An extremely affordable all-foam mattress that offers far more support than you’d expect for its price tag, a queen size Novilla Bliss is currently priced at $269.99 on both the brand’s own website and on Amazon. Keep an eye on prices as Black Friday approaches.

I tested the 10" version, but as detailed above, you can buy the Novilla Bliss in a variety of heights. But for this review, I’m concentrating on the middle ground of the 10” version. Starting at the top, there’s a breathable cover with OEKO-TEX certified fabric. This is helpfully removeable and washable — mattress covers that can’t be removed for freshening up are a real bugbear of mine, although I’d obviously recommend that you use a mattress protector anyway.

Underneath this is a layer of cooling memory foam that’s CertiPUR-US certified and contains the brand’s NanoGEL cooling particles, which Novilla says are designed to ‘capture and redirect excess body heat away from the surface’.

Next up is a layer of adaptive cushioning foam that provides comfort and a transition layer to the high-density support foam layer underneath it. This layer provides most of the support and prevents the mattress from sagging.

Underneath this you’ll find the zip to remove the top cover, plus a non-slip fabric to stop the mattress from sliding about on your bed base. Somewhat annoyingly, the mattress doesn’t have handles to help move it about but as it’s all-foam, it’s not impossible to rotate it without them.

As a lightweight sleeper, I rated the Novilla Bliss as a medium-firm mattress but my husband (and additional testers of a heavier build that I asked to try out the mattress) felt it was a medium, albeit a firmer medium. Averaging out scores, I’d probably place the mattress at a 6 out of 10 on the firmness scale.

There’s definitely some ‘squidge’ when you first lie on the mattress, but this is backed up by a decent amount of support from the lower levels. This combination makes it particularly suited for side sleepers. My husband in particular found the mattress instantly comfortable in this sleeping position, but it did take a couple of days for the foams to soften up a little at the shoulders for me — after this, it was extremely comfortable.

Pressure relief around the pressure points was also really good and I didn’t wake up with any symptoms of a dead hip (something that I can be prone to if the mattress is too unyielding).

I wasn’t expecting great things from this mattress when it came to sleeping on my back, as I’ve historically found all-foam mattresses can lack the firmer lumbar support that I find essential. And, when I first lay down on the bed, I did notice a tiny amount of pulling through my lower back. However, this eased quickly and as a lightweight sleeper, I actually found the mattress supportive enough to keep my spine aligned.

My husband, who boarders the lightweight and average weight category also found it pretty supportive. It’s not going to rival the very best mattresses for back pain but, overall, I thought it did an excellent job on pressure relief for both side and back sleeping.

If you’re of a heavier weight though, I don’t think you’ll find the Novilla Bliss supportive enough and even average weight sleepers towards the higher end of that weight bracket may find it lacks support for back sleeping. I asked a couple of friends who are larger than my husband and I to try the mattress out and while they both thought they could just about get away with it for side sleeping, they felt that support was lacking for both back and stomach sleeping.

In fact, strict stomach sleepers of any weight probably won’t get on with the Novilla Bliss as it’s just lacking in enough support to keep the hips lifted, leading to the spine sinking out of alignment. If you’re a stomach sleeper, have a look at our recommended mattresses for stomach sleepers instead.

I’m in the UK so the mattress was shipped over the Atlantic and, despite its long journey, it arrived none the worse for its voyage. Order on the Novilla website and you’ll receive a tracking number within two business days, with delivery within three to seven business days. Novilla uses FedEx, UPS and GOFO Express for delivery. If you order through Amazon, you can expect delivery in around five days and there’s also the option to pay for the delivery drivers to unpack the mattress and take away packaging.

I recruited my long-suffering husband to help get the mattress upstairs although, being all-foam, it was considerably lighter than the hybrid and pocket sprung mattresses I’ve tested in the past.

Once released from its vacuum seal, the Novilla Bliss did take longer than a hybrid mattress to inflate and I left it for a good 10 hours before sleeping on it. It did definitely continue to expand minutely over the next few days, so I’d say it was around 48 hours before it was fully expanded. The brand suggests that it will take 24-72 hours to fully expand, so this was bang on the money. Some Amazon customers have reported issues with the mattress not expanding fully but in fairness, I didn’t have any issues on this front.

Like most foam mattresses, there was some off-gassing from the Novilla Bliss. It wasn’t the worst I’ve come across but it did last for a couple of days.

My husband and I slept on the mattress for four weeks to get a clear overview of how it performed in key areas. In addition, I carried out some objective tests in an approximation of our comprehensive sleep lab testing methodology.

Through both objective and subjective testing, I’ve assessed the mattress in three key areas. I’ve looked at motion isolation (will a partner moving about at night disturb you?), temperature regulation (does the mattress keep a hot sleeper comfortable through the night?) and edge support (how solid does the edge of the bed feel when you lie right on it or sit on the mattress?). These are the results.

If you share your bed with a restless partner or are a light sleeper, a mattress with good motion isolation is a must. Good motion isolation stops movement from one side of the bed travelling over and waking up another sleeper. I can report back that the Novilla Bliss is particularly strong in this department.

My husband does tend to flail about in bed when he’s rolling over, channeling a walrus trying to leave the ocean and I’m a pretty light sleeper, so even a little motion transfer can be enough to wake me up. I’m pleased to report that I wasn’t disturbed by him at all during our testing period, which was an unusual and pleasing thing.

This was backed up by my objective tests. Firstly, I performed a series of drop tests. I placed a wine glass on the left-hand side of the mattress and dropped a weight from 24" above the bed surface on the right-hand side. This is a similar sensation to a person getting into bed.

I dropped the weight five times consecutively 30" away from the wine glass. Each time, the wine glass gave a very slight wobble but otherwise stayed upright, which was impressive. Next up, I got my husband to perform some subjective tests, starting with low force movements and then increasing to moderate and high force movements. I rated the mattress 10 out of 10 at low force and nine out of 10 at both moderate and high force. Overall, the Novilla Bliss really excelled when it came to motion isolation.

When I talk about temperature regulation, I’m looking at how well the mattress manages heat build-up throughout the night and whether it leaves a sleeper feeling stuffy. I’m afraid this was one area where the Novilla Bliss didn’t perform brilliantly, despite claims of a breathable cover and gel-infused memory foam.

My husband sleeps hot and he found the mattress stuffy after only 15 minutes of lying on it. And while he didn’t wake up seriously overheating, he did feel slightly clammy and uncomfortable. It was not a particularly breathable mattress and, on some hotter nights during testing, he did actually decamp to our spare room.

I’m something of a reptile at the best of times but even I noticed some heat building up around my lower back while lying on it. However, thanks to my cold nature, I wasn’t ever uncomfortable on it.

We tested through the tail end of an unusually warm period in the UK and through to some slightly cooler nights, so it gave me a good overall view of the mattress. For context, temperatures in the room ranged from around 75F down to 60F. However, I should point out that I wouldn’t expect an all-foam mattress to perform as well as a hybrid for temperature regulation and, if you are a hot sleeper, you’d be better off investing in one of our best cooling mattress picks.

A mattress with good edge support allows sleepers to use the whole width of the bed, as well as providing a stable surface to sit on while getting in and out of bed. My husband and I foster cats for a local charity and, as any cat servant will tell you, these little furry creatures have the ability to take up 90% of the bed overnight, leaving human subjects very much clinging to the edges.

Unfortunately, the Novilla Bliss wasn’t the strongest candidate when it came to edge support. There was some definite tilting when we lay on the edges, although I didn’t feel as if I’d actually fall off. It was a similar story when sitting on the edge of the bed — there was some definite tilting, but I didn’t feel as if I’d actually slip off.

To back up my experiences, I placed a 53lb weight midway across and 3" in from the foot and sides of the mattress. The weight sunk in by 5" immediately and dropped further to 6.5" after five minutes. And I had to get my husband to hold the weight the whole time (he only took his hands off very briefly for a photograph).

I repeated this test midway down and 3" in from the side of the mattress and got exactly the same results, with the weight needing to be held the whole time. Just for context, the same weight placed in the center of the mattress compressed by 5" immediately but then didn’t drop any further.

The Novilla Bliss receives overwhelmingly positive reviews from sleepers on both Amazon and the brand’s website. There’s lots of praise for the “exceptional” price and many sleepers praise it for its good quality. Sleepers also praise the mattress for pressure relief, with one customer describing it as the “perfect balance of softness and support…I woke up feeling much more rested without the usual aches and stiffness.” Overall, this is a recurrent theme, along with frequent praise for the motion isolation.

There are nearly 45,000 reviews for the mattress on Amazon so, as you might expect, you will find some complaints in there. The most common one seems to be poor expansion of the mattress, so it would seem that this might be something you’ll need to look out for. And, while many people praise the mattress for soothing aches and pains, stomach sleepers and those of a heavier build complain that the mattress is nowhere near supportive enough for their sleeping style or body weight.

✅ You’re a side sleeper of light or average weight: The Novilla Bliss excelled in pressure relief and comfort for side sleepers, easing tension and providing enough support for a really comfortable night’s sleep.

✅ You share your bed with a restless partner: There really wasn’t any motion transfer to speak of with the Novilla Bliss and I never felt disturbed by my husband moving about.✅ You’re on a budget: At $269.99 for a queen size, the Novilla Bliss is exceptionally good value for money and holds its own against some more expensive options.

❌You sleep on your stomach or are of a heavier build: The all-foam construction of the Novilla Bliss simply isn’t supportive enough for stomach sleepers or those who weigh over 230lbs. Try the Siena Signature mattress instead if you’re on a budget and fall into these categories.❌You’re a hot sleeper: The Novilla Bliss left my hot-sleeping husband feeling pretty stuffy and uncomfortable and its all-foam construction does trap heat a little too easily. The SweetNight CoolNest Memory Foam mattress offers excellent temperature regulation and is another budget option. ❌You need excellent edge support: The Novilla Bliss suffered with some sinkage at its edges and didn’t feel like the most secure surface to lie on the edge of or sit on. If you need an affordable mattress with decent edge support, check out the EGOHOME Black 12” Memory Foam mattress instead.

There are plenty of positives about the Novilla Bliss, but the price is the overwhelming winner. At under $300 for a queen, it’s a bit of a bargain and I was impressed by how well it performed considering that price tag. It certainly beats out quite a few more expensive mattresses when it comes to side sleeping in particular. The soft foams at the top and some decent support underneath mean that this is a great option for side sleepers, except for those of a heavier weight.

It also boasts some of the best motion isolation I’ve come across, and it will be a winner for co-sleepers thanks to this. But, as mentioned, I don’t think it’s a great fit for hot sleepers and I would like to see better edge support.

But overall, I was hugely impressed with this mattress, and I think that most lightweight and average side and back sleepers will be comfortable on this mattress.

This plush pillow is available in two sizes and two different firmness options. In our SquishPillow review, our tester found it best suited to side sleepers, which will match well with the Novilla Bliss. It's also only $29.99, so a bit of a bargain.

Rated the best bed sheets for hot sleepers by our bedding testers, these sheets are silky-soft and cool-to-touch — so they could help to make the Novilla Bliss a bit cooler to sleep on. And there are over a dozen colors/patterns to choose from.

Another way to help make a mattress cooler is to add a cooling mattress topper. The Lucid Gel Memory Foam mattress topper did a great job of keeping our tester cool and it's reasonably priced for such a nice thick topper. A thinner and cheaper 2" version could also save you some money.

When natural light isn't available, the best sunrise alarm clocks are the next best thing. You won't get a better gadget than the Hatch Restore 3 for this and, although it's not the cheapest purchase, it could really help to keep you happy through the winter months.

The best cheap option in our best weighted blankets round up, the YNM Original Cotton Weighted Blanket has a big choice of weights and lots of different colours to choose from - many of which are often dramatically reduced on Amazon.

Jo Plumridge is an experienced mattress reviewer with several years' experience covering all things mattresses and sleep, and who tests memory foam, hybrid and organic mattresses. What Jo doesn't know about a boxed mattress isn't worth knowing, so naturally we tasked her with producing a series of features for Tom's Guide looking at all aspects of mattresses, from how to pick between latex and memory foam (it's a tricky one), to the seven mistakes people make when buying a mattress for the first time. When testing the DreamCloud Luxury Hybrid for Tom's Guide, Jo said: "I loved the back support and pressure relief it offered. Plus, it looks far more expensive than it is." When she isn’t writing about sleep, Jo also writes extensively on interior design, home products and photography.

#3185. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous

Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead

• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress

Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”

Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”

Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.

Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities.

Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.

François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.

AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

Cal Newport is a computer science professor at Georgetown University where he is also a founding faculty member of the Center for Digital Ethics. He's the author of multiple bestselling books about human flourishing in a technological world and is the host of The Cal Newport Show podcast.

I think the current transformer attention method is not the method to reach ASI. There will need to be something else that pushes it forward. From my understanding the large data corpus is really just an advanced prediction system. Something will need to come along to actually understand concepts terms and know how to reason about things.

I think there's an element of expressing our values, even in the face of technological uncertainty, that this story gets at. We can still decide as a society that this handful of companies must develop their tech on terms defined by the rest of us. They may seem powerful and they are certainly telling us they intend to be even more powerful, but that's not the same as having political power today. I like Newport's idea that everyone else's voices matter, too.

#3184. Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:

In fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

#3183. Chase, Visa and Mastercard confirm vendor hacks as n0n leaks customer data

A ransomware gang has leaked about 16,000 email addresses tied to JPMorgan Chase’s invitation-only Reserve card, Cybernews found. The bank says the hack has nothing to do with Monday’s outage.

JPMorgan Chase says hackers got into data held by companies that work for the bank, and that it may include some customers’ names and email addresses. Visa and Mastercard have also confirmed incidents at outside providers.

We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack.

Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.

Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring.

There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week.

The bank said the attackers accessed marketing data held by those vendors. Its own services kept running. It will offer affected customers free credit monitoring where appropriate.

Chase also said the attack has no link to Monday’s outage, which it blamed on a software bug in its own hardware.

A ransomware gang called n0n published the data after a 48-hour deadline passed, Cybernews reported. Its researchers found about 16,000 customer email addresses, Chase account IDs and, in some cases, phone numbers. The file also holds 124 email addresses of bank staff.

All of the records seem to relate to Chase’s Reserve card, Cybernews said. The invitation-only Visa card is for wealthy clients, usually with at least $10m in managed assets.

“This association alone makes the leak a lot more sensitive,” said Aras Nazarovas, a senior security researcher at Cybernews.

The file is only 502KB. It is not clear whether it is a sample or all the gang took. TNW has not independently verified the data.

A Mastercard spokesperson told Business Insider that an outside provider exposed a limited number of email addresses. They belong to a small group of cardholders in one benefit programme. Mastercard said it has contained the exposure.

“There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards,” the spokesperson said.

Visa said its incident involved a service provider in the Asia Pacific region.

“Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected,” a Visa spokesperson said.

None of the three companies has named the vendors or said how many customers the breach hit.

n0n is a new gang, first tracked in mid-September, according to Cybernews. Last week it claimed to have stolen data from Expedia.

The leak comes at the end of a week of outages across the US. Wall Street executives and the NSA have reportedly blamed several of them on rushed security patches for flaws that AI found, not on hackers. Earlier this week, attackers also used Optimizely’s testing tool to plant malware on major websites.

#3182. Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers

This senior member’s chatbot helps them start agritourism businesses

Willie Jones covers transportation for IEEE Spectrum and the history of technology for The Institute.

Alice Dong has created an AI chatbot website that helps Colorado farmers plan and operate agribusinesses that draw visitors to their properties.

Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan CountyTitle Extension regional specialistMember grade Senior memberAlma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.

In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.

She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.

The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.

Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.

One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.

Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.

Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.

She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.

Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.

She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.

Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”

Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.

IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.

IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”

She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.

Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.

“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

Willie Jones is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum. In addition to editing and planning daily coverage, he manages several of Spectrum's newsletters and contributes regularly to the monthly Big Picture section that appears in the print edition.

#3181. Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign sounds like exactly what I’ve been wanting

Rumors about next year’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models have been ramping up, and they suggest Apple is designing an ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ that combines traits from two current models.

Apple keeps expanding the iPhone line to include new models. And while it’s great that there are more models for differing preferences and needs, it’s also left me missing the days of having one model that was the clear “best.”

That problem isn’t going away, since the iPhone Duo represents a brand new type of iPhone that some users will love, while others find it isn’t for them.

With my failed iPhone Duo experiment over, I’m back to using iPhone 18 Pro as my default model. But I still have an iPhone Air around for work, and every time I pick it up, I’m struck by how impressive it remains.

I used the iPhone Air all of last year and loved it. The main reason I upgraded to an iPhone 18 Pro is the camera system. I have young children at home—including newborn twins—and want to capture the best possible photos before they get older.

iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera has been fantastic, and it’s great having the Telephoto again too.

But I still sorely miss the overall design of the iPhone Air. And it sounds like next year, I could get the best of both models.

Rumors indicate Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models will have a unique new design featuring a quad-curved display that makes it look bezel-free.

The new models are expected to also be a bit slimmer, use curved edges, and possibly even bring back titanium. Leakers say the new design borrows a lot from the iPhone Air’s look.

This sounds like exactly what I’ve been hoping for.

While the ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ certainly won’t—and shouldn’t—be as thin as iPhone Air, if it can slim down a little and adopt several other Air design traits, I suspect it will evoke the same affection the Air has.

But unlike the Air, the new Pro model will still offer the best camera system in an iPhone (not to mention better battery life).

As a huge fan of the design of the Air, and the functionality of the 18 Pro, Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone model could prove the perfect model for me. And for anyone else not opting for iPhone Duo 2.

What do you think of the rumored iPhone 20 Pro design? Let us know in the comments.

#3178. Magnific passes $300M ARR and may raise outside money next year

Joaquín Cuenca told TNW that Magnific spends hundreds of millions of dollars on AI compute and runs Chinese video models. He wants to pass $1bn in revenue by the end of 2027.

Joaquín Cuenca, co-founder and CEO of Magnific.

Magnific, the Spanish AI creative platform once called Freepik, has not raised a funding round since 2010. Its customers have paid for everything, including the move into AI, co-founder and chief executive Joaquín Cuenca told TNW.

“On outside investment, we have no plans today, but nothing is set in stone. The investment this market requires is very significant, and if taking capital lets us accelerate, it may happen, maybe next year,” Cuenca said.

Magnific said on Tuesday that it has passed $300M in annual recurring revenue. It had $230M when it rebranded from Freepik in April. It is opening offices in Shanghai and Singapore and will spend $10M in Asia Pacific through early 2027.

Magnific says that makes it Europe’s fourth-largest generative AI company by ARR, on publicly reported figures. Only Lovable, ElevenLabs and Mistral rank higher. Mistral raised €3bn in September, and ElevenLabs doubled its valuation to $22bn in a share sale.

Magnific is still bootstrapped, Cuenca said. EQT took a majority stake in 2020. It bought shares from his partners and never put new money into the company.

Magnific is EBITDA positive, he said. Profit is thinner than revenue suggests, because most of the money goes straight back into AI compute. Every time a better image or video model comes out, users want it that same day, he added.

“We already spend hundreds of millions of dollars generating what our users ask for,” Cuenca said.

An IPO is not on the table today, Cuenca said. Public markets now ask for far bigger companies than they used to. His target is to pass $1bn in revenue by the end of next year. He expects to get there organically.

“What I value is that there is no timer on us,” Cuenca said.

Several of the best video models are Chinese, and users pick them because they win on quality, Cuenca said. Magnific runs ByteDance’s Seedance, Kuaishou’s Kling, Alibaba’s Wan and MiniMax’s models today.

Until last year he had never been to China, and Magnific’s suppliers were American. He has been several times since, once for just 20 hours. China entered Magnific’s top 10 markets this year for the first time.

Magnific is not trying to build its own foundation model to take on Google, ByteDance or OpenAI, Cuenca said. For an independent company, he called that “a lost battle”.

“Think of a MacBook: the models are the CPU, and we build the rest of the machine, the tools, the workflows, the controls,” Cuenca said.

The Shanghai office puts Magnific next to the teams that build those models, he said, so it can add new ones faster and pass on feedback from its users. According to the release, Singapore will be its sales base in the region, alongside existing teams in South Korea, Japan and Thailand.

“Studios need legal guarantees before they use anything in production, and meeting that bar is one of the reasons we are growing with them,” Cuenca said.

Magnific’s Enterprise plans include indemnification against third-party IP claims on what the platform produces, Cuenca said. Customers own what they create, and Magnific does not use their inputs or outputs to train models, he said.

“The exception is bad faith: if you ask for Mickey Mouse and you get Mickey Mouse, that’s on you,” he said.

In his view, responsibility has to move to the output. AI can infringe without the user meaning to, so what matters is detecting it and flagging it to the user.

“With any tool you can infringe: if you can draw two overlapping circles, you can infringe Mastercard’s trademark,” he said.

In Singapore, Hagia Labs made the films for telco StarHub’s Unlimited+ Plans campaign, with its creative partner Superson. StarHub’s green characters, the Hublings, fly across Asia and land in Japan. Hagia built the characters and settings in Magnific’s Spaces tool. Done the conventional way, Cuenca said, that would have meant travel, crews and a shoot in every location.

By Hagia’s own estimate, it took two to four weeks from brief to delivery. A conventional shoot would take two to four months.

Teams start by doing the same work faster, Cuenca said. Then they make what they could not afford before. Brands that used to advertise with a still image and a line of copy now make film-quality spots, and studios are greenlighting fantasy and historical projects that used to die on budget.

The next step is automation, he said. A team builds a workflow once in Spaces, and staff or their agents in ChatGPT or Claude can run it through Magnific’s MCP server.

Enterprise adoption in the region grew 35%, which is why Magnific is hiring there instead of flying people in from Málaga, Cuenca said. The release says Magnific plans more than 20 staff in Asia Pacific by the end of 2026, and twice that in 2027. Product and engineering stay at its Málaga headquarters. Cuenca called the offices “a long-term commitment to Asia” in Magnific’s release.

“Being funded by customers forces a discipline I don’t want to lose: you only build what people will pay for,” Cuenca said.

#3177. Apple releases iOS 27.3 public beta 2, new developer beta 2 build

Apple has released iOS 27.3 public beta 2 for iPhone. Today’s release also includes a new build for iOS 27.3 beta 2 for developers. The update brings new Calendar controls, more Siri AI capabilities, and new features for iPhone Duo. It also includes the redesigned Health app and other changes introduced earlier this month.

The update follows yesterday’s second developer beta and the first public beta on November 5.

Apple has also detailed higher daily usage limits for Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features through eligible iCloud+ plans. Plans with 200GB or more include extra capacity; the 50GB plan keeps standard limits.

See our full iOS 27.3 beta 2 roundup for more on the latest discoveries.

The first public beta brought back the redesigned Health app after its earlier preview during iOS 27.2 testing. On iPhones with Apple Intelligence support, Insights collects trends across your health data, while Longevity includes a Health Age comparison based on Apple Watch measurements.

If you’re already testing the public beta, open Settings > General > Software Update to check for the new version.

Joining for the first time? Make a backup, then enroll in the free Apple Beta Software Program using your iPhone’s Apple Account. In Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, choose iOS 27 Public Beta. Go back to Software Update to download and install it.

#3175. PBF Energy: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Yield upgrades and tight global supplies position the company to expand margins without major capital outlays.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than PBF Energy ›

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 29, 2026, PBF Energy (PBF -1.30%) announced a net debt reduction of more than $1.2 billion for the quarter. Debt paydown protects balance sheet health against commodity market volatility.

PBF Energy has eliminated more than $2 billion in net debt, which measures total borrowings minus cash balances, so far this year. Replacing high-cost senior notes with lower-cost financing significantly lowers ongoing borrowing costs and expands through-the-cycle cash flow.

Under its Refining Business Improvement program, an internal cost-reduction and operational efficiency initiative, PBF Energy directs capital toward high-return product yield upgrades. Targeting minor process modifications instead of high-cost refinery expansions preserves capital while increasing high-value fuel output.

Global refining capacity remains constrained by facility shutdowns and inventory levels well below historical norms. Tight product supplies benefit complex coastal refiners that process diverse crude slates and meet regional fuel demand.

Operational execution and completed refinery maintenance give the system an unencumbered operating path into year end. Complex asset configuration and crude slate flexibility protect refining margins while management maintains strict operational discipline.

Strategic priority remains focused on plant reliability, yield optimization, and debt reduction to deepen financial resilience across volatile energy cycles.

#3174. First macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4 RCs rolling out [U: Public]

Update, November 19, 4:46 p.m. ET: The release candidates are now available to public beta testers, with the same build numbers as the developer RCs.

In addition to macOS 27.3 beta 2, Apple is also rolling out the first Release Candidates for macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4. Here are the details.

Two weeks ago, Apple released macOS Tahoe 26.7.3 and Sequoia 15.8.3, along with macOS 27.2.1 Golden Gate, all of which included security fixes related to AirPlay, Bluetooth, and Messages, among others.

Today, the company released the first RCs for macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4, along with the second developer beta for macOS 27.3.

As is usually the case with direct-to-RC rollouts, Apple’s notes mention only that the updates provide ”security fixes for your Mac.” The actual release notes will likely become available soon after Apple officially releases macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4 in the coming weeks.

The build for macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 RC 1 is 24H319, and the build for macOS Tahoe 26.7.4 RC 1 is 25G422.

Did you spot anything new in today’s RCs? Let us know in the comments.
